{{Short description|Mathematical inequality related to Nesbitt's}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Shapiro inequality''' is an [[inequality (mathematics)|inequality]] proposed by [[Harold S. Shapiro]] in 1954.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Shapiro |first1=H. S. |last2=Bellman |first2=R. |last3=Newman |first3=D. J. |last4=Weissblum |first4=W. E. |last5=Smith |first5=H. R. |last6=Coxeter |first6=H. S. M. |date=1954 |title=Problems for Solution: 4603-4607 |url=https://doi.org/10.2307/2307617 |journal=The American Mathematical Monthly |volume=61 |issue=8 |pages=571 |doi=10.2307/2307617 |jstor=2307617 |access-date=2021-09-23|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

==Statement of the inequality==

Suppose {{Mvar|n}} is a [[natural number]] and {{Math|''x''<sub>1</sub>, ''x''<sub>2</sub>, &mldr;, ''x''<sub>''n''</sub>}} are [[positive number]]s and:

* {{Mvar|n}} is [[parity (mathematics)|even]] and less than or equal to {{Math|12}}, or
* {{Mvar|n}} is [[parity (mathematics)|odd]] and less than or equal to {{Math|23}}.

Then the '''Shapiro inequality''' states that

:<math>\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{x_i}{x_{i+1}+x_{i+2}} \geq \frac{n}{2},</math>

where {{Math|1=''x''<sub>''n''+1</sub> = ''x''<sub>1</sub>}} and {{Math|1=''x''<sub>''n''+2</sub> = ''x''<sub>2</sub>}}.  The special case with {{Math|1=''n'' = 3}} is [[Nesbitt's inequality]].

For greater values of {{Mvar|n}} the inequality does not hold, and the strict [[lower bound]] is {{Math|''&gamma;'' {{sfrac|''n''|2}}}} with {{Math|''&gamma;'' &approx; 0.9891&mldr;}} {{OEIS|A245330}}.

The initial [[mathematical proof|proofs]] of the inequality in the pivotal cases {{Math|1=''n'' = 12}}<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Godunova |first1=E. K. |last2=Levin |first2=V. I. |date=1976-06-01 |title=A cyclic sum with 12 terms |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01149930 |journal=Mathematical Notes of the Academy of Sciences of the USSR |language=en |volume=19 |issue=6 |pages=510–517 |doi=10.1007/BF01149930 |issn=1573-8876|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and {{Math|1=''n'' = 23}}<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Troesch |first=B. A. |date=1989 |title=The Validity of Shapiro's Cyclic Inequality |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2008728 |journal=Mathematics of Computation |volume=53 |issue=188 |pages=657–664 |doi=10.2307/2008728 |jstor=2008728 |issn=0025-5718|url-access=subscription }}</ref> rely on numerical computations. In 2002, P.J. Bushell and J.B. McLeod published an analytical proof for&nbsp;{{Math|1=''n'' = 12}}.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bushell |first1=P. J. |last2=McLeod |first2=J. B. |date=2002 |title=Shapiro's cyclic inequality for even ''n'' |url=https://zbmath.org/?q=1018.26010 |journal=Journal of Inequalities and Applications |language=English |volume=7 |issue=3 |pages=331–348 |doi=10.1155/S1025583402000164 |doi-access=free |issn=1029-242X}}</ref>

The value of {{Math|''&gamma;''}} was determined in 1971 by [[Vladimir Drinfeld]].  Specifically, he proved that the strict lower bound {{Math|''&gamma;''}} is given by {{Math|''&psi;''(0)}}, where the [[function (mathematics)|function]] {{Mvar|&psi;}} is the [[convex hull]] of {{Math|1=''f''(''x'') = ''e''<sup>&minus;''x''</sup>}} and {{Math|1=''g''(''x'') = 2 / (''e''<sup>''x''</sup> + ''e''<sup>''x''/2</sup>)}}. (That is, the region above the [[graph of a function|graph]] of {{Mvar|&psi;}} is the convex hull of the [[union (set theory)|union]] of the regions above the graphs of {{Mvar|f}} and {{Mvar|g}}.)<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Drinfel'd|first=V. G.|date=1971-02-01|title=A cyclic inequality|url=https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01316982|journal=Mathematical Notes of the Academy of Sciences of the USSR|language=en|volume=9|issue=2|pages=68–71|doi=10.1007/BF01316982|s2cid=121786805|issn=1573-8876|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{MathWorld|ShapirosCyclicSumConstant|Shapiro's Cyclic Sum Constant}}</ref>

Interior local minima of the left-hand side are always {{Math|&ge; ''n'' / 2}}.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Nowosad |first=Pedro |date=September 1968 |title=Isoperimetric eigenvalue problems in algebras |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/cpa.3160210502 |journal=Communications on Pure and Applied Mathematics |language=en |volume=21 |issue=5 |pages=401–465 |doi=10.1002/cpa.3160210502 |issn=0010-3640|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Similar to [[Nesbitt’s inequality]], there is no corresponding [[upper bound]] as the cyclic sum [[inequality (mathematics)|inequality]] can be made arbitrarily large.

==Counter-examples for higher ''n''==

The first [[counter-example]] was found by Lighthill in 1956, for {{Math|1=''n'' = 20}}:<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Lighthill |first=M. J. |date=1956 |title=An Invalid Inequality |url=https://doi.org/10.1080/00029890.1956.11988785 |journal=American Mathematical Monthly |volume=63 |issue=3 |pages=191–192|doi=10.1080/00029890.1956.11988785 |url-access=subscription }}</ref>
:<math>x_{20} = (1+5\epsilon,\ 6\epsilon,\ 1+4\epsilon,\ 5\epsilon,\ 1+3\epsilon,\ 4\epsilon,\ 1+2\epsilon,\ 3\epsilon,\ 1+\epsilon,\ 2\epsilon,\ 1+2\epsilon,\ \epsilon,\ 1+3\epsilon,\ 2\epsilon,\ 1+4\epsilon,\ 3\epsilon,\ 1+5\epsilon,\ 4\epsilon,\ 1+6\epsilon,\ 5\epsilon),</math>
where <math>\epsilon</math> is close to 0.  Then the left-hand side is equal to <math>10 - \epsilon^2 + O(\epsilon^3)</math>, thus lower than 10 when <math>\epsilon</math> is small enough.

The following counter-example for {{Math|1=''n'' = 14}} is by Troesch (1985):
:<math>x_{14} = (0, 42, 2, 42, 4, 41, 5, 39, 4, 38, 2, 38, 0, 40)</math> (Troesch, 1985)<!--this example has been double-checked by user:FvdP, 2010/01/12-->
<!-- Next counter-example is cited in A M Fink 1998 as from Troesch 1985. Sadly, it seems wrong: I compute LHS = 0.50010878... there probably is a typo in it.
